As my Deputy Executive Director mentioned in her opening remarks, we have established that terrorist groups like Daesh and al-Qaeda and their affiliates do exploit political instability, ongoing conflicts, porous borders, food and security in formal economies and can also benefit from territorial control in some areas that comes with then access to various types of resources that are present in those territories. Terrorist groups also continue to reorganize and expand their financial networks, adapting very quickly to enforcement measures but also— also exploiting regulatory and operational gaps. And this is really a huge challenge for countries with lower institutional and operational capacities, as well as countries weakened by conflicts and terrorist activity. CETA analysis— and this is also reflected in our annual assessments of gaps in the implementation of key CFT requirements, which we publish annually. Annually, as its name suggests, shows that while legal frameworks on CFT are improving, effectiveness of the implementation remains very uneven. CTAD identifies persistent weaknesses in national risk assessments, which are often outdated, inconsistent, or disconnected from broader CFT strategies. Terrorism financing investigations and prosecutions remain very limited, with financial intelligence units and law enforcement authorities lacking the capacity and the coordination to pursue complex cases. Furthermore, links between terrorism financing and organized crime, including such types of crimes as trafficking and illegal mining, are insufficiently analyzed, and the oversight of affected economic sectors remain weak. Informal and cash-based economies, including, for example, mobile money service providers and money value transfer system or alternative remittance networks, remain the preferred means for moving funds undetected. In combination, emerging technologies add further risks, but in-depth assessments and investigations legislative capacity does not measure up to those challenges. Oversight of these sectors as well must be reinforced through effective regulation and public-private partnerships. We've also noted a particular concern about the continuous challenge to counter and address financing issues related to foreign terrorist fighters with networks using sophisticated technologies and informal channels combined to raise and move funds to allow for their movements. Implementation of targeted financial sanctions also lags, hampered by weak designation processes, delays in freezing assets, and limited cross-border cooperation. Most governments still lack systems to analyze or share data on cross-border cash movements, making detection rare. Next slide, please. So what do we do to address all these problems? Harmonizing legal networks globally helps reducing opportunities for terrorist organizations to benefit from regulatory discrepancies and loopholes. Effective cooperation in terrorism financing investigations and prosecutions based on coherent criminalization of the offense and robust information-sharing channels compliant with international law is also essential to dismantle terrorist networks operating in multiple jurisdictions, which is almost very frequently, at least, if not almost always the case. Multilateral designations of terrorist organizations, notably under the UN Security Council sanction regime, still appear as the most overreaching sanction instrument to obstruct terrorism financing, especially in relation to tackling transnational TF schemes. Dear Excellencies, distinguished The delegates and partners, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to begin by expressing Interpol's sincere gratitude to the Kingdom of Bahrain and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and to our colleagues from the Islamic Military Counterterrorism Coalition and UNOCT for co-organizing this side event and for inviting Interpol to contribute to this this discussion. One of the defining trends of our era is the shift toward decentralized technology-enabled financing. This demands new tools, new reflexes, and enhanced international cooperation. Through its Global Law Enforcement Network, Interpol stands ready to assist member countries by providing the tools and secure cooperation mechanisms needed to address these emerging threats together. We have played a crucial role in supporting the implementation of the UN Global Counterterrorism Strategy over the past 20 years, helping member countries strengthen their capacity based on FATF's standards and respond to CTED's technical recommendations. We are a bridge translating policy into practice alongside member countries and our partners. Let me highlight concrete, concrete examples of what this looks like. Operation Catalyst, conducted last year in partnership with AFRIPOL, was a landmark operation targeting terrorism financing across 6 African countries. Authorities screened more than 15,000 persons of interest, arrested 83, 83 individuals, and uncovered about $260 million, including in virtual currencies, with links to terrorism-related activities. The operation also highlighted the expanding nexus between terrorism and organized crime and demonstrated how these threats increasingly transcend national boundaries and exploit international connectivity. In Kenya, a suspected money laundering operation using a virtual asset, asset service provider, was identified as having potential links to terrorism financing. In a separate case, two individuals were arrested for the online recruitment of young people from East and North Africa into terrorist groups, with funds traced through a cryptocurrency trading platform back to individuals in Tanzania. A second example speaks to the value of cross-border casework on a smaller scale. In 2025, one of our member countries in Europe requested assistance with a live terrorist financing investigation in which the suspect had financed the travel of family members and others to conflict zones by transferring funds of approximately €18,000. Our specialized officers liaised with 4 other member countries across Africa, the Americas, and the Middle East where funds had been transferred. At the request of the investigating country, Interpol published a red notice for the suspect, who was subsequently arrested in other member country and extradited for prosecution. €18,000, 5 countries, 3 continents, 1 suspect. That is the geometry of modern terrorist financing, and it is why no country can fight in it alone. Allow me to turn now to three specific instruments that are reshaping how Interpol combats terrorism financing and at the operational level. The first is IGRIP, Interpol's Global Rapid Intervention of Payments stop payment mechanism. This mechanism is designed to facilitate real-time cooperation between countries, enabling them to trace, intercept, and freeze criminal proceeds quickly. When a suspicious transaction is identified, information is shared instantly through Interpol's secure channels, allowing involved member countries to act before funds move beyond reach. Since its launch in 2022, member countries have used EuGrip to intercept more than $200 million stemming largely from cyber-enabled fraud. In one operation, authorities were, were able to block over 82,000 suspicious bank accounts. Seizing a combined total of $300 million, including $200 million in hard currency and over $100 million in virtual assets. iGrip is not just a financial crime tool. It is a counter-terrorism tool because the same illicit financial channels are increasingly exploited by both organized crime group— criminal groups and terrorist actors. The second instrument is i-FUSE Connect. One of the most persistent structural weaknesses in counterterrorism financing is the gap between financial intelligence units and law enforcement. FUSE holds critical data. Suspicious transaction reports, financial profiles, and asset trails. But that data has historically been silent, silent from the police databases where it could generate the most actionable intelligence. Interpol is championing the extension of i24/7, our secure global police communication system to fuse across the world and promoting the systematic inclusion of financial information in Interpol alerts related to terrorist subjects of interest. I-FU Connect takes this further, giving financial intelligence units direct access to Interpol's databases, connecting the dots between financial red flags and known terrorist profiles in real time. When iView in one country flags a suspicious bullet, iView Connect allows that signal, signal to be cross-referenced against Interpol's global holdings immediately rather than weeks later through a formal request. Speed matters. Impunity thrives in the gap between detection and action. Finally, the third instrument is the Silver Notice, Interpol's latest color code notice launched in January 2025. It allows police in over 80 countries to publicly request information of illegal assets and thus facilitates the tracing and identification of criminal assets for seizure or recovery. Today, we have seen great successes in rolling out the Silver Notice. We currently have over 200 active Silver Notice requests seeking to trace a total of $2.2 billion. US dollars in assets, with more than 2,500 responses shared by participant countries and over $40 million in assets already traced or identified. We encourage all member countries to make full and systematic use of this instrument. Together, IGrip, IFU Connect, and the silver notice represent a new generation of financial intelligence infrastructure built for the speed, decentralization, and digital character of today's threat environment. But we must also honestly confront what is not yet working. Asset recovery rates remain very low—2%, according to recent reports. Meaning that 98% of the proceeds of financial crime are never identified or recovered. That figure is true for terrorist financing as it is for organized crime. There is also the persistent challenge of information silos. Financial intelligence held by one agency in one country, in one country, sorry, rarely reaches the investigators who need it in another country in time to matter. Delayed sharing is a pressing concern. It is the gap through which terrorist financing flows. Interpol calls all member countries to strengthen financial intelligence units, invest in the technical capacity of law enforcement agencies and make full use of Interpol's channels and tools, including iGrip, iViewConnect, and the Silver Notice, to facilitate the timely, real-time exchange of information across borders. The threat is structural, and so must be our answer. That means breaking down silos investing in financial intelligence capacity, and making use of every tool available, including those Interpol has built precisely for this purpose. I thank you very much.

Your Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. It's an honor to be part of this side event on behalf of Kenya's Financial Intelligence Unit, and I want to express our sincere gratitude to the organizers for convening this timely and vital side event, and specifically for the IMCTC for the invitation to share our experiences. For Kenya, evolving TF threats are not a theoretical challenge but an operational reality. Today, I want to share how Kenya translates global obligations into practical, effective measures that respond to our national risks while safeguarding financial inclusion and humanitarian operations. As we confront evolving global TF threats, We must recognize that a one rigid, one size fits all enforcement model is not only ineffective in low capacity and exposed contexts, but it is also counterproductive. So now, how do we ensure that CT and CFT implementation is truly risk-based and tailored to national contexts rather than being mechanically prepared? So for Kenya, This answer lies in dynamic, data-driven risk understanding. So risk understanding must be dynamic, reflecting the evolving terrorist financing typologies, domestic threats, and sector vulnerabilities. So this means that financial institutions should be empowered and should be allowed to justify controls through documented risk analysis rather than blanket measures that lead to to mass de-risking. In Kenya, our National Terrorism Financing Risk Assessment has allowed competent authorities and reporting institutions to identify exactly where elevated risk lies. So this allows us to direct our regulatory resources strategically to high-risk areas rather than dispersing supervisory efforts equally across all sectors. This targeted approach is sustained by continuous collaborative dialogue and feedback loops between the regulators and the private sector through guidance, typology reports, and feedback to ensure that the risk-based decisions are both consistent and responsive to our national realities? Secondly, how do we reinforce these regulatory systems without creating unintended barriers to financial inclusion? So for many developing economies, especially and particularly in Kenya, financial inclusion itself is a core security objective. So when we have individuals and small businesses excluded from the financial system, they often migrate to informal channels where transactions become significantly more difficult to monitor. Kenyans' mobile money ecosystem demonstrates that financial inclusion and financial integrity can reinforce one another. So we do this through the robust customer identification, transaction monitoring, and reporting mechanism that have expanded access while also strengthening transparency. So rather than viewing innovation as a threat, Kenyan regulators manage emerging risks without undermining financial inclusion. So regulation must and does facilitate access when mitigating risks, utilizing simplified customer due diligence for lower-risk transactions to keep vulnerable populations within the formal financial safety net while still maintaining financial integrity. Thirdly, our framework must protect the legitimate operations of humanitarian actors in fragile settings. Humanitarian organizations often operate in high-risk environments affected by conflict and weak governance. However, a blanket application of CFT restriction can choke off vital funds. So guided by the United Nations guidance on human rights and countering terrorist financing, Kenya actively rejects the narrative that the entire NPO sector is is inherently high risk. So our regulatory frameworks are designed to isolate specific vulnerabilities than— rather than penalizing the— an entire sector. Domestic coordination is also vital in ensuring that a risk-based and proportionate approach is applied to deal with these identified risks. In conclusion, security and financial inclusion must coexist. Framework that cause financial exclusion or block aid only fuel the marginalization that terrorist networks exploit. But effective implementation of these CFT obligations demands strong national capabilities. This is why international organizations like the IMCTC, the UNCCCT, and the UNOCT play a vital role in strengthening national capabilities through specialized training, knowledge sharing, and institutional capacity building. Kenya has proactively sought this partnership, including the requesting participation in the IMCTC, reflecting its commitment to strengthen national resilience, adopt national— international best practices, and collectively— and contribute to the collective global security. Thank you all.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, as terrorist financing continues to evolve, We are seeing a widening gap in many low-capacity and vulnerable jurisdictions between emerging risk and the capacity to respond effectively. As noted earlier by CTED, many member states are still in the process of developing the legal and regulatory frameworks necessary to comply with international law, including FATF recommendations, while the terrorist financing landscape is evolving rapidly through, in particular, the increasing use of new technologies. Emerging financial technologies and new terrorist financing behaviors are reshaping the environment in which member states pursue security, financial integrity, and sustainable development. These developments affect not only how we detect and disrupt terrorist financing, but also how we safeguard financial inclusion, humanitarian action, and the rule of law. We see today populations that are already among the most vulnerable facing a threat that is evolving faster than the institutions responsible for addressing it. Closing this gap is hence an urgent priority, but it must be done in a way that strengthens, not undermines, financial inclusion and preserves threatens the operational space on which communities and humanitarian actors depend. From UNCCD perspective, in delivering technical assistance on countering the financing of terrorism, several implementation realities deserve a particular attention. And I'll echo here Kenya by mentioning that the risk-based approach, first, as the cornerstone of the FATF Recommendation 1.. In many low-capacity jurisdictions, translating this principle into practice remains, however, a significant challenge. As Dr. Abdullah from IMCC already noted, national authorities are often expected to put in place CFT measures with limited means, limited statistics and data, and without the analytical infrastructure needed to fully understand their own risk. Landscape. And this is precisely where CTED's assessments and mutual evaluations against the FATF standards are essential for our capacity-building mandate at UNCCCT. Those reports provide the evidence base that enables us to support the member states in developing frameworks that reflect their specific risk context rather than replicating models— designed for very different operating environments. Closely linked to this principle of risk-based is the proportionality. Both Security Council Resolution 2462 and FATF recommendation, notably the 8th recommendation, underscore that CFT measures should avoid unintended consequences, including financial exclusion de-risking and undue risk— restrictions, sorry, on civil society. In fragile contexts, CFT measures introduced with security objectives can disrupt remittance channels, exclude rural communities from the formal financial system, or impede humanitarian operations. Effective implementation therefore requires measures that are carefully calibrated. Integrated. And for this reason, UNCCD places particular emphasis on mitigating, de-risking, promoting financial inclusion and reinclusion in the near future, supporting the operation— operationalization of humanitarian exemptions. And we also assist member states in designing frameworks that enable financial institutions to maintain services in higher-risk environments, or apply customer due diligence and facilitate the work of legitimate non-profit organizations without imposing disproportionate compliance burdens. And these are fundamental elements of balanced implementations that we all pursue. And finally, no CFT framework can be effective without stronger and more structured engagement with the private sector. That has been also said previously. And in many low-capacity contexts, banks and money transfer operators are often the first to identify suspicious transactions, but they are also the first to withdraw services when regulatory expectations or risk profiles remain unclear. So strengthening public Private partnerships enables authorities to share typologies, clarify expectations, and reduce the uncertainty of— that often drive de-risking. And these partnerships are not simply beneficial, they are indispensable to the effective implementation of proportionate and risk-based CFT framework. It's just about applying them in a way that strengthens resilience, protects financial inclusion, and preserves the humanitarian space on which vulnerable communities depend. With these partners, UNCCD stands ready to continue supporting member states in building CFT systems that are effective in practice, proportionate to risk, and fully aligned with the international obligations.

Thank you very much, Secretary-General. I'll try very briefly to summarize today's discussion that reaffirmed several important messages. First, terrorist financing remains an evolving and adapting threat. It exploits gaps in capacity, regulation, technology, coordination, and geography. In low-capacity and exposed contexts, these gaps are especially difficult to address when institutions are under pressure and resources are limited. Secondly, capacity building must be practical and linked to operational impact. International standards and national frameworks are essential, but their value depends on whether they help authorities identify risks, use financial intelligence, investigate and prosecute cases, disrupt networks, and cooperate across borders. Thirdly, support to member states must be tailored to context. Low-capacity and exposed environments require approaches that are realistic, sequenced and responsive to national priorities, and partnerships that connect policy guidance with operational tools, technical assistance, and regional cooperation. Fourthly, balanced implementation is central to sustainable effectiveness. Risk-based, proportionate, and context-sensitive measures strengthen the legitimacy and precision of counterterrorism efforts. They help protect financial inclusion, inclusion, preserve humanitarian space, safeguard legitimate civil society activity, and ensure compliance with international law and support humanitarian exemptions. This is where also UNOCT and UNCCT have a very important role to play. We will continue to advance policy coordination, support implementation of the Counter-Terror Strategy, and promote coherence across the United Nations system. And through the Centre, we will continue to help Member States strengthen counter-terrorism frameworks, enhance operational cooperation, and implement international standards in a manner that is effective, proportionate, and adapted to national realities. As we continue with the Counter-Terrorism Week, today's discussion reminds us that the implementation of the Counter-Terrorism Strategy must remain connected to realities on the ground, where coherent, practical, and sustained support is most needed. I really hope that the insights shared today, really from everybody, will inform our continued cooperation beyond this week and contribute to a more resilient and inclusive society.
